Making diffusion models on networks

Source: R/class_play.R, R/make_diffusion.R
make_play.Rd

These functions simulate diffusion or compartment models upon a network.

  • play_diffusion() runs a single simulation of a compartment model, allowing the results to be visualised and examined.

These functions allow both a full range of compartment models, as well as simplex and complex diffusion to be simulated upon a network.

as_diffusion(.data, attribute = "diffusion", twomode = FALSE, events)

play_diffusion(
  .data,
  attribute = "diffusion",
  transitions = NULL,
  steps,
  ...,
  seeds = 1,
  compartments = NULL,
  contact = NULL,
  direction = c("in", "out", "all"),
  prevalence = 0,
  background = 0,
  threshold = 1,
  transmissibility = 1,
  onset = 1,
  recovery = 0,
  waning = 0,
  fatality = 0,
  immune = NULL,
  old_version = FALSE,
  thresholds,
  latency
)

Arguments

.data

An object of a {manynet}-consistent class:

  • adjacency or incidence matrix from {base} R

  • edgelist data.frame from {base} R or tbl/tbl_df from {tibble}

  • stocnet stocnet, from the {manynet} package

  • igraph igraph, from the {igraph} package

  • network network, from the {network} package

  • tidygraph tbl_graph, from the {tidygraph} package

attribute

The name of the categorical node attribute that holds the state of each node. By default "diffusion". See the section "Start state". For as_diffusion(), the attribute whose changes record the diffusion: the report has one column for each of its values.

twomode

Not used. Kept for compatibility.

events

A table (data frame or tibble) of diffusion events with columns t indicating the time (typically an integer) of the event, nodes indicating the number or name of the node involved in the event, and event, which can take on the values "I" for an infection event, "E" for an exposure event, or "R" for a recovery event.

transitions

A data frame of the transitions between the values of attribute. See the section "Transitions". By default NULL, which uses the model that the other arguments set.

steps

The number of steps forward in the diffusion to play, after the start. By default the number of nodes in the network, or the period of data that change in time. If steps = Inf then the diffusion process will continue until a step in which no node changes state, after the last wave and the last change to active.

...

Not used. Any argument given here gives an error, with the nearest argument name.

seeds

The nodes that start as infected, when attribute is not on the nodes. An index, a logical vector the length of the number of nodes, one or more node labels, or the name of a logical node attribute. By default the first node.

compartments

A named vector or list that maps the roles S, E, I, R, and D onto the values of attribute. By default NULL, which maps each role onto itself. See the section "Start state".

contact

A matrix or network that replaces ".data" with some other explicit contact network, e.g. create_components(.data, membership = node_in_structural(.data)). Can be of arbitrary complexity, but must of the same dimensions as .data. A panel, an event stream, or a list of networks is followed in time, as ".data" is.

direction

Which ties expose a node, from the view of the node at risk. "in" (the default) counts the ties that infected nodes send to it, "out" counts the ties that it sends to infected nodes, and "all" counts both. On an undirected network, the three are the same.

prevalence

How much the share of infected nodes in the whole network lowers each node's threshold, from 0 to 1. The threshold becomes threshold * (1 - prevalence * share), where share is the share of the live nodes that are infected at the start of the step. By default 0, which means that there is no global mechanism.

background

The probability that a susceptible node becomes infected at a step without any exposure, its background rate of infection or innovation. This is similar to the coefficient of innovation in the Bass model. By default 0, which means that a node is infected only through its contacts.

threshold

A numeric vector indicating the threshold each node has. By default 1. A single number means a generic threshold; for thresholds that vary among the population please use a vector the length of the number of nodes in the network. If 1 or larger, the threshold is interpreted as a simple count of the number of contacts/exposures sufficient for infection. If less than 1, the threshold is fractional: the proportion of contacts that must be infected. The name of a numeric node attribute is also accepted.

transmissibility

The transmission rate probability, \(\beta\). By default 1, which means any node for which the threshold is met or exceeded will become infected. Anything lower means a correspondingly lower probability of adoption, even when the threshold is met or exceeded.

onset

The probability that an exposed node (infected, but not yet infectious) becomes infectious at a step, \(\sigma\). For example, if exposed individuals take, on average, four days to become infectious, then \(\sigma = 0.25\), as for recovery. By default 1, which means those exposed become immediately infectious, and there is no exposed compartment (i.e. an SI model). Anything lower results in e.g. a SEI model.

recovery

The probability those who are infected recover, \(\gamma\). For example, if infected individuals take, on average, four days to recover, then \(\gamma = 0.25\). By default 0, which means there is no recovery (i.e. an SI model). Anything higher results in an SIR model.

waning

The probability those who are recovered become susceptible again, \(\xi\). For example, if recovered individuals take, on average, four days to lose their immunity, then \(\xi = 0.25\). By default 0, which means any recovered individuals retain lifelong immunity (i.e. an SIR model). Anything higher results in e.g. a SIRS model. \(\xi = 1\) would mean there is no period of immunity, e.g. an SIS model.

fatality

The probability those who are infected are removed from the network, \(\alpha\). Note that fatality is distinct from a natural mortality rate. By default \(\alpha = 0\), which means that there is no fatality. Where \(\alpha > 0\), the nodal attribute 'active' will be added if it is not already present. A node that dies no longer infects others, and cannot be infected again.

immune

A logical or numeric vector identifying nodes that begin the diffusion process as already recovered. This could be interpreted as those who are vaccinated or equivalent. Note however that a waning parameter will affect these nodes too. By default NULL, indicating that no nodes begin immune.

old_version

This is included to maintain backward compatibility with the old version of this function, that would return a special object. The new version adds the diffusion event record as changes to the original network.

thresholds, latency

Superseded on 2026-11-14, and give a warning from 2.6.0. Use threshold (the name of the column in transitions, and of the argument in netrics::node_by_contagion()) and onset = 1 - latency instead.

Value

as_diffusion() returns a 'diffusionModel' object (with the class 'diff_model' second, for compatibility), a table of the number of nodes in each value of the attribute at each step, from the start of the diffusion. The table has a column for each value, and a column of the new nodes in each value (for example I and I_new). A record in S, E, I, and R always has these four columns, and s counts the susceptible nodes that are exposed. A node that dies, as from fatality, becomes inactive, and is counted in the value of D (and D_new) from then on, and not in the value it held when it died. Any other node that is not active is not counted, and n counts the nodes that are counted at each step. Until 2.6.0, a column t also copies time, but is not printed. The table keeps the name of the attribute in attr(, "attribute"), and the roles of its values in attr(, "compartments"), where these are known. By default, a compact version of the component table is printed (to print all the changes at each time point, use print(..., verbose = T)). To retrieve the diffusion events table, use summary(...).

Simple and complex diffusion

By default, the function will simulate a simple diffusion process in which some infectious disease or idea diffuses from seeds through contacts at some constant rate (transmissibility).

These seeds can be specified by a vector index (the number of the position of each node in the network that should serve as a seed) or as a logical vector where TRUE is interpreted as already infected.

threshold can be set such that adoption/infection requires more than one (the default) contact already being infected. This parameter also accepts a vector so that thresholds can vary. A threshold of 1 gives a simple contagion, which one contact can pass on. A threshold of 2 or more gives a complex contagion (Centola and Macy 2007), which needs several contacts to reinforce one another.

A threshold less than one is a fractional threshold: the share of the node's contacts that must be infected. A fractional threshold is not always complex: a threshold of 0.1 on a node with five contacts needs only one of them. A node with no contacts never reaches a fractional threshold, so it adopts only as a seed or from background.

Nodes that cannot be infected can be indicated as immune with a logical vector or index, similar to how seeds are identified. Note that immune nodes are interpreted internally as Recovered (R) and are thus subject to waning (see below).

Compartment models

Compartment models are flexible models of diffusion or contagion, where nodes are compartmentalised into one of two or more categories.

The most basic model is the SI model. The SI model is the default in play_diffusion()/play_diffusions(), where nodes can only move from the Susceptible (S) category to the Infected (I) category. Whether nodes move from S to I depends on whether they are exposed to the infection, for instance through a contact, the transmissibility of the disease, and their threshold to the disease.

Another common model is the SIR model. Here nodes move from S to I, as above, but additionally they can move from I to a Recovered (R) status. The probability that an infected node recovers at a timepoint is controlled by the recovery parameter.

The next most common models are the SIS and SIRS models. Here nodes move from S to I or additionally to R, as above, but additionally they can move from I or R back to a Susceptible (S) state. This probability is governed by the waning parameter. Where recover > 0 and waning = 1, the Recovery (R) state will be skipped and the node will return immediately to the Susceptible (S) compartment.

Lastly, these functions also offer the possibility of specifying a latent period in which nodes have been infected but are not yet infectious. Where onset < 1, an additional Exposed (E) compartment is introduced, and onset is the probability that a node moves from this E compartment to infectiousness (I) at each step. This can be used in in SEI, SEIS, SEIR, and SEIRS models.

Start state

The state of each node is held in a categorical node attribute, named by attribute (by default "diffusion"). The diffusion starts from this attribute in one of three ways, in this order:

  1. The attribute has changes recorded on the network: the diffusion continues this history from its last time, and the history stays in the record. Observed times of adoption can be added first with bind_changes().

  2. The attribute is on the nodes, but has no changes: its values are the start state, at the first time of the network. A logical attribute reads TRUE as infected (I) and FALSE as susceptible (S).

  3. The attribute is not on the nodes: all nodes start as susceptible, seeds start as infected, and immune nodes start as recovered, at the first time of the network.

The first time of the network is the earliest time of its ties, or 0 for a network whose ties have no time. seeds and immune are used only in the third case. A node whose state is missing (NA) starts as susceptible. In the first two cases, the record holds only the changes after the start, because the attribute already holds the start state.

compartments maps the roles of the model (S, E, I, R, and D) onto the values of the attribute, for example compartments = c(S = "unaware", I = "adopter"). Only the roles that the model uses must be given: S and I always, R for recovery or immune, E for onset, and D for fatality. Several values can share a role, as in compartments = list(S = c("Conservative", "Moderate"), I = "Liberal"). The first value of a role is the one that the record writes. By default, each role is its own value.

Transitions

A diffusion moves the nodes between the values of attribute. transitions gives these moves as a data frame, with one row for each transition and these columns:

  • from and to: the value that a node leaves, and the value it goes to.

  • rate: the hazard per step, 0 or more (Inf is certain). A number, a number for each node, the name of a numeric node attribute, or a function of state, exposure, time and .data that returns a hazard for each node at each step. A function replaces the exposure model of its row.

  • source: the value that causes the transition, or NA (the default) for a spontaneous transition. Several values, as in "E+I" or as a list column, count together.

  • exposure: how the contacts in source give the hazard. "threshold" (the default) gives rate to each node with at least threshold such contacts. "cascade" gives each such contact its own chance, so the hazard is rate times the number of contacts. "voter" gives rate times the share of contacts in source.

  • threshold: the number of contacts in source (1 or more), or their share (less than 1), that a node needs. By default 1. A number, a number for each node, or the name of a node attribute.

  • prevalence: how much the share of all nodes in source lowers the threshold, as in threshold * (1 - prevalence * share). By default 0.

A node moves with probability \(1 - e^{-\sum h}\) over the rows that it can take, and its destination is drawn in proportion to their hazards. Rows with the same from and to add their hazards. In each step, the spontaneous transitions (rows with no source) occur first, from the state at the start of the step. The other transitions then count only the contacts that are still in source, so a node that recovers or dies in a step does not infect others in that step. Each value that the attribute holds must be in at least one row. For a value that never changes, add a row with rate = 0.

Without transitions, the arguments after ... give the table. They are chances per step, and each chance \(p\) becomes the hazard \(-\log(1 - p)\). With transitions, these arguments are ignored, with a warning.

For example, the voter model on two values: data.frame(from = c("Liberal", "Conservative"), to = c("Conservative", "Liberal"), rate = 1, source = c("Conservative", "Liberal"), exposure = "voter").

Time and composition

A diffusion follows the time of the ties. On a panel, each wave stays in force until the next wave, and the last wave stays in force after the end. A list of networks with the same nodes is a panel, with one wave for each step. On an event stream, a tie can transmit only once it occurs, and an interval tie only while it is active. A network whose ties or changes are dated plays one step for each day. By default, data that change in time run until one step after their last moment, and a list of networks runs one step for each network.

In a two-mode network, a state that is known on one mode only (on the nodes, in their history, or from seeds and immune) diffuses on that mode only, through co-affiliation: a node is exposed by the infected nodes with which it shares a node of the other mode, while that node is active. The nodes of the other mode have no state. A state on both modes diffuses along the ties between the two modes.

A node with active = FALSE is not at risk and does not transmit. Changes to active take effect at their time. Use active = FALSE to exclude a node whose state is not known. A node that dies (D) becomes inactive in the record.

A 'stocnet' keeps the table of transitions in info$transitions.

Assumptions

The models make these assumptions, which an analysis may need to state:

  • Time is in discrete steps, and all nodes update at once, from the states at the start of the step (synchronous updates).

  • Each argument after ... is a chance per step, such as transmissibility or recovery. So the mean time in a state is \(1/p\) steps, from a geometric distribution, and the chance does not change with the time spent in it.

  • Exposure follows the ties in direction. An unweighted tie counts each infected contact once. A weighted or signed tie adds its weight, and a fractional threshold divides by the sum of the weights. The layers of a multiplex network are combined first, as as_matrix() combines them.

  • A threshold gates a fixed chance. Under "threshold" exposure, a node over its threshold adopts with the same chance however far over it is. Use exposure = "cascade" in transitions for a chance from each contact.

  • Nodes do not decide: no node adopts because of what it expects others to do, and no node changes its ties in response to the diffusion.

  • A node with active = FALSE is out of the model: it is not at risk and does not transmit.

Arguments that set the model

The arguments after ... are shortcuts that set the default model. Give them by their full name. A name that is not one of these arguments gives an error, with the nearest argument name.

References

On simple and complex contagion

Centola, Damon, and Michael Macy. 2007. "Complex contagions and the weakness of long ties", American Journal of Sociology, 113(3): 702-734. doi:10.1086/521848

Examples

  # How to create a diffusionModel from (basic) observed data
  events <- data.frame(time = c(0,1,1,2,3),
                       node = c(1,2,3,2,4),
                       var = "diffusion",
                       value = c("I","I","I","R","I"))
  as_diffusion(bind_changes(create_filled(4), events))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>    time     S     I     R
#>   <int> <int> <int> <int>
#> 1     0     3     1     0
#> 2     1     1     3     0
#> 3     2     1     2     1
#> 4     3     0     3     1
  smeg <- generate_smallworld(15, 0.025)
  play_diffusion(smeg, seeds = 1, recovery = 0.2)
#> 
#> ── # Small-world network ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> # A undirected network of 15 nodes and 30 ties
#>

#>   <chr>    
#> 1 S        
#> 2 S        
#> 3 S        
#> 4 S        
#> # ℹ 11 more rows
#> 
#> ── Changes 
#> # A tibble: 29 × 4
#>    time  node var        value
#>   <dbl> <int> <chr>     <list>
#> 1     0     1 diffusion I<chr>
#> 2     1     2 diffusion I<chr>
#> 3     1     3 diffusion I<chr>
#> 4     1    14 diffusion I<chr>
#> # ℹ 25 more rows
#> 
#> ── Ties 
#> # A tibble: 30 × 2

#>   <int> <int>

#> 3     3     4
#> 4     4     5
#> # ℹ 26 more rows

  # A start state from an attribute, in labels of its own
  smeg <- mutate_nodes(smeg, aware = rep(c("yes", "no", "no"), 5))
  play_diffusion(smeg, "aware", steps = 5,
                 compartments = c(S = "no", I = "yes"))

                 transitions = data.frame(from = "associate", to = "partner",
                                          rate = 0.1))
